prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in such moire systems

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is, in my reading, the cleanest discovery on the shortlist: a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model giving flat bands near a specific twist angle) followed seven years later by experiments showing correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. This is the pattern of finding clues in nature and then identifying the people behind them. It created a field, moire quantum materials, with a single tunable structural knob, and the results have been reproduced across many groups and platforms. The theory-plus-experiment split gives a natural three-person prize that fits the statutes without strain, and the opening ballots show unusually broad support (first place from three members, top eight from all eight).
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is maturity of interpretation: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated phases are still debated, so the prize would honour a discovery whose physical explanation is unsettled. There is also a real priority question on the theory side (earlier moire band-structure work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) and on the experimental side (Cao as lead author, and Dean and Yacoby and others in closely related work). If the committee concludes that the field needs several more years to settle, optical lattice clocks (B049) or topological insulators (B026) are better established.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first: the magic-wavelength concept is clearly Katori's, Ye's group brought the clocks to the 1e-18 level, the field is mature after twenty years, and recognition would be timely.
responses.response: I agree that B049 has the cleanest attribution on the list and the most solid maturity case, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. I place it below B009 because it is an advance in how well we can measure rather than a new phenomenon, and because it sits in the same lineage as the 2005 and 2012 prizes. You argue it is timely, and I accept that, but a prize on a mature metrology result can wait for the redefinition of the second, whereas the moire result is a new state of matter that is clearly attributable now. Your point on Lemonde and Ludlow is a fair caveat that applies to B049 more than the twisted-graphene credit applies to B009.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first on the strength of a falsifiable theory-to-experiment chain and about two decades of confirmation, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D contributors are outside the supplied credit.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and with your own caution about attribution. My difficulty is that the credit problem is acute rather than marginal: the HgTe observation followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is not credited, Zhang has died, and the 3D work by Fu, Kane, Moore, Hasan and others is a separate achievement. A Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize would be defensible but would leave visible gaps, whereas the B009 split between theory and experiment has fewer such gaps. I would not oppose B026 if the committee can find a citation that handles the HgTe step honestly, but I do not think it is easier to allocate than twisted graphene.

responses.point: Ranks twisted bilayer graphene eighth, saying it is outside his specialty and may be early because the superconducting mechanism and many phases are still evolving, and that credit is spread across many experimental groups.
responses.response: The point about early timing deserves a serious answer. I distinguish the discovery from its interpretation: the existence of flat bands at the predicted angle and of correlated and superconducting states is robustly reproduced, and earlier prizes have honoured experimentally established phenomena whose microscopic origin was not settled. I do not think the open pairing question makes the prize premature, but I accept that it is the main reason someone might wait. On credit spread, I would answer that the committee's task is to identify decisive contributions, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero group's 2018 observation are those, even though Dean and others contributed.

responses.point: Ranks active-matter hydrodynamics first as a conceptually unified field spanning Vicsek, Toner-Tu and Ramaswamy, while also ranking twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I take the active-matter case seriously as a statistical-physics concept, and I am glad B009 is your second choice, but B011 has no support from other members and a credit problem I find hard to settle: Yuhai Tu is outside the credited names, so the Toner-Tu theory would be recognised through Toner alone. I also see no single decisive experiment comparable to the twisted-graphene observation. I would want to hear which experimental results you regard as the confirming discoveries before treating B011 as a competitor to the top candidates.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first while acknowledging possible bias from proximity to the field, and noting that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in time.
responses.response: I appreciate that you state your closeness to the field openly. I think the 2025 prize makes B040 a harder sell now, because the committee would be rewarding superconducting-circuit physics in consecutive years. The distinction between the tunnelling work and the strong-coupling architecture is real, but I would rank B040 behind several candidates that have no such overlap. I would also note that Girvin and Devoret are outside the credited names, which weakens the three-person configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the unsettled origin of the superconductivity and correlated phases makes recognition early compared with B049 or B026.

How the committee should treat earlier moire band-structure work (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and the experimental groups beyond Jarillo-Herrero, and whether the proposed citation should be framed to protect against that.

Whether a two-part prize combining a theory-and-experiment moire prize with another candidate would be preferable to a single three-person prize; I do not currently see a combination that keeps the union within three people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited names for B009, B049, B026 or B012 is among my documented connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group). My own field is high-energy theory and cosmology, so I am assessing condensed-matter and AMO candidates from outside my specialty.
